short: A distributed directory that answers questions about domain names.
detail: A DNS question includes a name and record type. DNS can return addresses, aliases and delegations. A cache hit can avoid one or more network round trips.
design: DNS gives services a stable name while addresses change. Measure cold and warm lookup latency separately and include cached answers in rollout timelines.

short: A stores an IPv4 address. AAAA stores an IPv6 address.
detail: The record sets are distinct even when they belong to the same hostname. A dual-stack client can ask for both and choose which address to connect to.
design: Test both families independently. A healthy IPv4 deployment can still publish a broken IPv6 path.

short: An alias that names another hostname.
detail: For an address lookup, the resolver follows the alias to its target and needs an A or AAAA record there. The two record sets have independent TTLs.
design: Aliases make provider changes easier, but long chains increase cold latency and add dependencies on other zones.

short: A record naming a nameserver for a DNS zone.
detail: A parent zone uses NS records to delegate a child zone. A child zone also publishes an authoritative NS set at its apex. The parent can supply glue addresses when resolution would otherwise depend on the child.
design: Keep parent and child delegation data consistent. A nameserver migration can be limited by delegation and glue lifetimes even if answer TTLs are short.

short: A zone record with administrative data and timing parameters.
detail: Start of Authority (SOA) carries the zone serial, refresh parameters and MINIMUM. Negative answer TTL uses the smaller of the SOA record TTL and SOA.MINIMUM.
design: Choose negative cache lifetimes alongside provisioning deadlines. A long negative TTL can hide newly created names during rollout.

short: The client-side DNS interface that normally asks a recursive resolver.
detail: The OS may have a local DNS cache. On a miss the stub sends a recursive question to its configured resolver. Some browsers use an independent resolver path.
design: App, OS and client policies can differ. Reproduce lookup behavior with the same client stack that showed the incident.

short: A DNS service that completes a lookup for its clients.
detail: It checks its cache and follows referrals as needed, usually making a series of iterative queries. It stores records by their own lifetimes.
design: Shared recursion cuts internet traffic and latency. Its cache and availability affect many clients, so measure the resolver itself as well as your authority.

short: An authoritative server for the DNS root zone, written as a dot.
detail: Root hints bootstrap a recursive resolver. For a question under .com, a root server normally points the resolver to the .com nameservers.
design: For ordinary name lookups the root is mostly a cold-start dependency because delegations are widely cached.

short: The rightmost label under the DNS root, such as .com.
detail: A TLD nameserver is authoritative for its own zone and refers the resolver to separately managed child zones such as example.com.
design: Registrar-level delegation and your zone’s records sit in different control planes. Test both during nameserver changes.

short: A server responsible for answering from a particular DNS zone.
detail: For a name in its zone the server can return a record set, authoritative absence, or a referral when the name lies below a delegation.
design: Monitor authoritative QPS and failures. Policy changes there affect new lookups and will be observed at different times as downstream caches refresh.

short: A DNS reply pointing the resolver to servers closer to the answer.
detail: A referral usually carries the child zone’s NS records in the authority section, sometimes with glue address records. The recursive resolver sends another query.
design: Delegations can remain warm when an address expires. Plan delegation changes independently from service record changes.

short: How long a cache may ordinarily reuse a record.
detail: Browser, OS and recursive caches each track remaining TTL in seconds. Changing the advertised TTL affects new answers. Some clients apply local floors or stale-answer policies.
design: For a migration, publish the lower TTL at least one old TTL in advance, then verify the old population has drained.

short: Saving an answer that a name or requested record is absent.
detail: A cached NXDOMAIN applies to name and class across query types. NODATA is specific to a missing record type at an existing name.
design: Negative caching protects authorities from repeated misses but can delay the visibility of a fix. Include newly provisioned names in propagation checks.

short: The DNS response code for a name that does not exist.
detail: An authoritative negative response includes the zone SOA for cache timing. An existing name that lacks the requested type is a separate NODATA case.
design: Distinguish name absence from timeout or server failure. The remediation and the persistence of cached results differ.

short: Returning a different service address when the usual target is unhealthy.
detail: Health checks update the authority’s view, after which a new lookup can get an alternate address. Clients may still hold a cached IP or reuse existing connections.
design: Plan recovery time for detection, cache drain and client retries. DNS alone rarely guarantees a hard upper bound.

short: A probe used to decide whether a backend should receive new traffic.
detail: Probe intervals and consecutive failures set detection delay. Checks can test transport reachability or application readiness depending on what failure should trigger a switch.
design: Probe the dependency whose loss should change routing. Tune hysteresis to avoid oscillation and verify the backup can handle the full load.

short: Choosing an answer based on where a query appears to come from or how fast a site is for that location.
detail: The authority usually sees the recursive resolver’s address. EDNS Client Subnet can convey a client prefix where supported, at the cost of additional cache partitioning and privacy exposure.
design: Measure routing from actual user networks. A far-away or shared resolver can make an apparently local policy return a poor address.

short: Several sites offer the same IP address and routing selects a reachable site.
detail: Sites advertise a common prefix. BGP path selection can lead different users to different sites with the same DNS answer. Advertisement changes converge through the network.
design: Tie withdrawal to service health. Expect some convergence delay and account for stateful connections that might break during a route change.

short: The protocol networks use to exchange IP reachability and select routes.
detail: Networks announce prefixes and apply policy to choose paths. Announcements and withdrawals take time to propagate and do not guarantee selection by geographic distance or RTT.
design: Coordinate route changes with application health and monitor from multiple networks. Convergence is separate from DNS caching.

short: A distributed fleet of edge sites that serve users near their networks.
detail: A CDN can cache eligible responses and proxy other requests. The edges can terminate TLS and reuse connections to the application origin.
design: Separate latency, request offload and byte offload goals. Dynamic routes may benefit from acceleration even at zero cache hit ratio.

short: One location in a CDN where user traffic enters or content can be cached.
detail: PoPs typically hold independent working sets. A hit in one region does not fill a different region unless a shared tier or proactive distribution is used.
design: More PoPs can shorten user paths while increasing duplicate cold fills. A shared shield can absorb the resulting fan-out.

short: The upstream application or storage service a CDN fetches from.
detail: The origin serves dynamic responses and supplies misses or validations. This lab counts origin requests and successful response body bytes. The shield lab measures peak origin RPS in one-second buckets aligned to the burst start.
design: Budget the origin for cold caches and invalidations. A healthy warm-cache hit ratio can hide a capacity problem during rollout.

term: Cache hit, miss and hit ratio
short: A hit uses a cached response. A miss needs a fill. An expired copy may need validation or qualify for stale service.
detail: The lab divides fresh hits by all completed requests, including errors, bypasses, stale responses and validations.
design: Compare hit ratios across similar traffic classes and check byte offload too. Large misses can dominate bandwidth even when the request hit ratio is high.

short: The share of user requests that did not require a separate origin request.
detail: Compare origin fetches with incoming user requests for the same burst. Hits and collapsed followers can both improve request offload. Byte offload also depends on body sizes and revalidation.
design: Measure offload at the origin boundary. Edge misses can still be inexpensive when the shield has a hit or a shared fill.

short: HTTP directives that govern storage, freshness and reuse.
detail: A response can give shared and private caches different freshness limits. Unqualified private allows private caches only. No-store tells recipients to avoid storage.
design: Set explicit policy per route. Default personal responses to a policy that prevents shared caching and verify what the edge actually receives.

short: The freshness lifetime in seconds for a cached HTTP response.
detail: The cache compares current age with the freshness lifetime. Downstream shared caches should account for the age already accumulated upstream.
design: Choose freshness according to the tolerated age of content. Longer lifetimes improve reuse and make changing a stable URL slower to observe.

short: A freshness lifetime that overrides max-age in shared HTTP caches.
detail: Browsers still apply their own freshness policy. Once stale, a shared cache applying s-maxage requires validation for further reuse under the normal HTTP cache rules.
design: Set a longer shared lifetime when you want strong CDN reuse and quicker browser refreshes. Confirm the policy at both tiers.

short: The request identity used to decide which stored response can be reused.
detail: Keys generally include the target URI and can include selected query parameters, cookies or headers. Vary adds matching requirements for request headers.
design: Include every dimension that changes the representation. Strip only proven irrelevant dimensions and measure hit ratio by key cardinality.

short: A response header telling caches which request headers influence the representation.
detail: Vary: Accept-Language means a cache matches the new request against the language header of the stored request. Vary: * prevents a normal cached match.
design: Keep negotiation inputs small and intentional. High-cardinality headers fragment the cache while missing variation can serve the wrong response.

short: A validator that identifies a selected representation of a resource.
detail: A cache can send its ETag in If-None-Match. For a matching GET or HEAD, the origin can return 304 and the cache updates its stored metadata.
design: Generate validators consistently across origin replicas. Changing a validator while bytes stay the same prevents useful revalidation.

short: A conditional response that allows a client or cache to reuse its stored body.
detail: A 304 carries metadata and no representation body. A shared cache can use it to refresh stored metadata, then serve a complete response from the stored bytes.
design: Expect 304 to save bandwidth and still consume origin round trips and request handling. Watch both origin QPS and bytes.

short: A bounded window in which a cache can serve stale data while it refreshes asynchronously.
detail: An eligible request can trigger a background fetch while it immediately receives the stored body. A successful validation or fill updates the cache for later requests.
design: Use SWR where a small freshness lag is acceptable. It moves revalidation latency off the hot path and softens synchronized expiry.

short: A bounded window in which a cache can serve a stale copy when fetching fails.
detail: An eligible upstream error, such as HTTP 503, lets the cache fall back to stored content while the grace period is open.
design: Set grace periods according to how long old content stays useful. Monitor stale serves separately so a resilient edge cannot hide an origin outage.

short: Invalidating selected CDN copies before their normal expiry.
detail: Providers can support keys, paths or tags, with different propagation and in-flight semantics. The lab models a hard local purge of the selected tiers.
design: Purge narrowly and budget the cold traffic it creates. Large invalidations can synchronize misses across PoPs.

short: A URL containing a fingerprint or version that changes when the contents change.
detail: Publish each version under a new URL and keep old bytes available until old references disappear. An immutable cache directive discourages validation during the fresh lifetime.
design: Give immutable assets long freshness and update the documents that point to them separately. Retain old versions for in-flight pages and rollbacks.

short: A shared upstream cache that serves misses from several CDN edges.
detail: An edge miss goes to a common intermediate point. A shield hit avoids an origin trip, and a collapsing shield can also deduplicate concurrent cold fills.
design: Place the shield where edges and origin can reach it reliably. Size and isolate it as an origin protection layer with its own failure domain.

short: An arrangement where a cache asks an upstream cache before reaching the source.
detail: Edges can share a larger or longer-lived working set upstream. A hit there keeps origin off the path, while a cold miss can pay an extra hop.
design: Pick tiers from request locality and available capacity. Preserve response age between tiers so a copied response does not accidentally get a new full TTL.

short: Sharing one in-flight fetch among concurrent requests for the same cache key.
detail: A leader fetches while followers wait. The safe sharing boundary includes cache key and eligibility. If the leader fails, followers need a bounded failure or retry strategy.
design: Collapse at the scope where duplicate work accumulates. Per-PoP deduplication leaves cross-PoP duplicates unless they meet at a shared tier.

short: A burst of similar work arriving together at an upstream system.
detail: A synchronized cache expiry, purge or deploy can turn ordinary traffic into many concurrent origin misses for the same object.
design: Test realistic cold release and purge scenarios. Combine collapsing, jitter or prewarming with enough origin capacity for genuinely distinct misses.

short: The CDN accepts the client’s encrypted connection at a nearby PoP.
detail: The CDN can use a separate secured upstream connection to origin. Reusing this connection avoids repeated TCP and TLS handshakes across the longer path.
design: Measure connection reuse and client handshake latency independently of cache hits. Preserve trust boundaries on both legs when proxying sensitive traffic.
